privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: This page explains in plain language what personal data Labour Market AI uses, why it uses it, and what rights you have. It describes the platform as it works today, before payments are active.

sections.heading: What data the platform uses
items: Account data: your email address and the sign-in linked to it.
Content you enter yourself: profile and CV details, skills, work journal entries, photos you attach to entries, and the documents you list in your document inventory.
Company information entered by company users: company details, needs, projects and bookings.
Messages you send and receive on the platform.
Consent records: when you give or revoke a consent, the action and its time are stored.
Technical data needed to run the service, such as sign-in cookies (see the Cookie Policy).

sections.heading: What the data is used for
items: To run the features you use: profile and CV, work journal, skill suggestions you confirm, market map, projects, teams, bookings and messaging.
To show your information only to people an explicit access rule allows — see the page “Your data and who can see it”.
To keep an honest history of consents and key access changes.
The platform does not use third-party advertising or analytics trackers and does not build behavioural profiles.

sections.heading: Who can see your data
items: Access is closed by default: data you enter belongs to your account, and other users see nothing unless a specific rule allows it.
Worker documents are not shown to employers or agencies without the worker's consent, and employers cannot read a worker's saved locations.
Messages are visible only to the participants of the conversation.
The full plain-language summary is on the page “Your data and who can see it”.

sections.heading: Consent
items: Where a feature shares data further, it asks for your explicit consent first.
You can revoke a consent at any time. Revocation is recorded: the consent history is kept as an audit trail instead of being erased, so it stays clear who agreed to what and when.

sections.heading: Your rights
items: You can ask to see the data held about you, to correct it, to receive a copy of it, to restrict how it is used, or to have it deleted.
Honest current state: these requests are handled manually. There is no self-service export or deletion button yet — contact us and a person will process your request.
Where processing is based on consent, you can withdraw that consent at any time.

sections.heading: How long data is kept
items: Data is kept while your account is active and the feature it belongs to still uses it.
Consent and audit records are kept as history: a revocation is recorded rather than the record being erased.
Exact retention periods are part of the final legal wording that is still being prepared.

dataProtection.title: Data protection
dataProtection.intro: This page explains in plain words how data inside Labour Market AI is protected. It describes only what is actually built into the platform today.

sections.heading: Closed by default
items: User data tables are protected by access rules inside the database itself. If no rule explicitly grants access, the data is not visible — even to other signed-in users.
These rules work at the database layer, not only in the interface, and are covered by automated tests.

sections.heading: History instead of silent changes
items: Access grants are records, not switches: when access is withdrawn, the record is marked as revoked instead of being deleted, so history stays traceable.
Consent history is kept the same way.

sections.heading: No trackers, no profiling
items: The platform contains no third-party advertising or analytics trackers, no session-recording tools and no behavioural scoring.

sections.heading: Statistics that protect individuals
items: Market statistics are aggregated. Averages are not shown for samples so small that they could point to a single person, and small samples are flagged.
Research-type data sets are structurally anonymous: they contain no names, email addresses or personal identifiers.

sections.heading: Files and photos
items: Photos and files are kept in private storage and opened through short-lived links, not public addresses.

sections.heading: Administrator access
items: Administrator screens are limited to a small set of platform administrators and fail closed: without the administrator role they are not reachable.

sections.heading: Export and deletion
items: Export and deletion requests are handled manually today: contact us and a person will process your request.

sections.heading: Honest limits
items: No system can promise absolute security. If you notice a problem, contact us — a person will review it.

sections.heading: What workers can see about companies
items: Workers see what a company chooses to publish: public needs and offers appear only after moderation.

sections.heading: Messages
items: A conversation is visible only to its participants. Colleagues from the same company who are not participants see nothing — not even that the conversation exists.
If an extra person is granted access (for example the object owner), that access lasts only while the grant is active. When it is revoked, access ends, and the history stays recorded.

sections.heading: Administrators
items: A small set of platform administrators can see the operational queues needed to run the platform, such as support and review queues. Administrator pages are restricted and fail closed.

sections.heading: If something looks wrong
items: The access rules in the database are the source of truth, and this page follows them. If something here does not match what you see, contact us — a person will review it.

matrix.title: Permission matrix: who can see and change what
matrix.intro: The table below lists the main product surfaces and, for each role, what that role can see and what it can change. It is written from the actual access rules in the database and in the route guards — each row points to the exact rule that enforces it. Where a rule is narrower than a short label can express, the row's note explains the boundary in plain words.
matrix.sourceNote: The "Rule" line under each row names the file in the codebase (a database policy, function or route guard) that enforces the row. These references are technical on purpose — they let anyone check that this page claims nothing broader than what the rules actually do.

profileAccount.editNote: You change only your own profile. Administrators can correct records when needed.

workerCard.seeNote: Companies see an anonymised preview only — no name and no contact details without the worker's permission. The worker sees their own full card.
workerCard.editNote: Only the worker (and, when needed, an administrator) can change the card.

workJournal.editNote: Entries cannot be rewritten after saving. The worker adds their own entries; managers add review results, not edits.

orgMembership.editNote: You manage your own membership records; administrators handle corrections.

messaging.heading: Who can message whom
messaging.intro: Every direct conversation must match exactly one of the rules below. There is no generic "allowed" — each permission names the real relationship behind it, and the default is closed.

rules.existingConversation: People who already share an active conversation can continue it.
rules.engagement: A company and a worker with a real employment or engagement link can message each other.
rules.scoutingShortlist: A company can open a conversation with a scouted worker only if the company owns the related need, the worker is on its shortlist, and the worker is currently contactable.
rules.admin: Platform administrators can open support conversations.

about.metaDescription: A plain-language explanation of Labour Market AI: how workers build a real profile from real work, how companies describe needs and find teams, and how the platform stays honest.
about.title: What Labour Market AI is and how it works
about.lede: Labour Market AI is a labour-market platform where workers, companies and teams show real skills, see real needs and organise real work — locally and across Europe.
about.honesty: Everything described on this page exists in the product today. Features still being prepared are named as such, and payments are not active yet.

loops.heading: For workers
points: You create your profile — your player card — with your skills and experience.
You keep a work journal: short entries about the work you actually did.
The platform reads your journal text and suggests skills it recognises. Recognition is rule-based, it can miss things, and nothing is added to your profile without your confirmation.
Your profile shows honestly how each skill is supported: entered by you, supported by journal entries, or confirmed by people you actually worked with.

loops.heading: For companies
points: You describe your need: what work, where and when.
You see the market map and honest market signals instead of promises.
You can scout for workers: profiles appear anonymised, and contact happens only with permission.
Projects, teams and bookings keep the work organised in one place.

loops.heading: For teams and communication
points: Teams and brigades are managed inside the company workspace.
Work instructions can be written in your own language — the original text is always kept, and nothing pretends to be translated when it is not.
Messaging is closed by default: only the participants of a conversation can see it.

notYet.heading: What the platform does not do
points: It does not mark anyone as confirmed by itself — a confirmed status always comes from a real person.
Payments do not run through the platform yet, and there is no checkout.
It does not give legal advice. Document guidance is informational only.

sportsModel.heading: The operating model: player cards, teams and objects
sportsModel.intro: The product borrows sports vocabulary because it makes work organisation visible. It is an operating model, not a game — every layer below is a real product surface.

rows.meaning: A worker's capability card: real skills, real work evidence, and confirmations that always come from real people.
A real work unit inside a company — created and managed in the company workspace.
The field of play: the place where work actually happens and where workers are assigned.
The person who manages assignments: who works on which object, and when an assignment ends.
Optional grouping and status layers for markets and professions — the platform uses them to group, never to rank.
